analysis.one_liner: Bars gas companies from using eminent domain to take land for LNG export pipelines or state-owned land.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in September 2020, it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, a gas company that wins a federal permit to build an interstate pipeline can go to federal court and use eminent domain to take private land along the route, paying the owner. This bill would change that in two ways: it would bar federal courts from condemning any land in which a state government owns an interest, and it would ban companies from using eminent domain at all for pipelines built mainly to ship natural gas to terminals for export overseas. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners in the path of proposed LNG export pipelines, who would no longer face condemnation of their homes, farms, and forests for projects whose profits flow from foreign sales. State governments would also gain, because land they own — parks, forests, wildlife areas — could no longer be condemned by a pipeline company in federal court.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the holder of a federal pipeline certificate from exercising eminent domain for a project built substantially to move natural gas to an LNG terminal or otherwise export gas abroad.
Strips U.S. district courts of jurisdiction to condemn property in which a state owns any interest, protecting publicly owned parks, forests, and conservation land from pipeline condemnation.

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas pipeline developers and LNG export companies, who would lose a federal power — eminent domain — that currently lets them assemble pipeline rights-of-way over private and state-owned land. Gas producers and export terminals could also face slower or fewer pipeline routes to overseas markets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas pipeline and LNG export companies

drawbacks.text: The ban applies only to export-oriented pipelines; a company could still use federal eminent domain to condemn land for a domestic pipeline, so landowners on non-export routes get no new protection.

Supporters of pipeline projects argue that eminent domain comes with court-supervised compensation and that restricting it for export routes would raise construction costs, complicate route planning, and slow gas infrastructure even where landowners are fairly paid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For landowners and state-owned land, the protection is direct and substantial: it removes the single most feared tool pipeline companies use against property owners on export routes. The cost falls on pipeline and export companies through harder, costlier rights-of-way, and the bill is narrow — it leaves the broader eminent-domain system for domestic pipelines untouched, so it is a partial fix rather than a comprehensive one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 23, 2020 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day, and the Congress ended with the committee never holding a hearing or vote on it.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced S. 4680 on September 23, 2020, joined by Senator Ron Wyden as its sole cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced.
No further action was taken: the action history lists no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas pipeline companies and LNG exporters are better off, because they keep the federal eminent-domain power the bill would have taken away for export pipelines, and landowners and state landholding agencies remain exposed to condemnation. The bill's two Senate sponsors gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gas pipeline and LNG export companies

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end the use of federal eminent domain for LNG export pipelines and for land in which states hold an interest.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, took no action on the bill; it received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators were ever attached to the bill, both Democrats, and there were no votes, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would remove their power to condemn private land in federal court for export pipelines and any land in which a state holds an interest. Their gain under current law comes directly at the expense of the property owners whose land is taken.
Export-focused pipelines could no longer use eminent domain to assemble rights-of-way, making routes to LNG terminals harder and costlier to build. Overseas sales profits depend on those routes.
